paras: The burning of a Mojave woman accused of witchcraft was the reported killing, in late summer 1888, of an unnamed Mojave woman of about eighteen by members of her tribe in eastern San Bernardino County, California. According to the reports, the band's leaders judged her a witch, and she was tied to a stake and burned, dying after about two hours. The story reached the press through two Los Angeles accounts in mid-September and ran nationally under headlines about Indian "barbarism" and revived witch burning.

One account came from Frank Semon, a former Los Angeles policeman back from some months on the Colorado River, who put the burning near Rock Springs "about three weeks" before a dispatch dated September 16. The other, a San Francisco dispatch credited to "good authority at Los Angeles" and to ranchers who had visited the Indian camp, said a "strange disease" had attacked the tribe for two months. Its fullest form, in the Richmond Dispatch, said at least twenty men of the tribe had died of the illness, which the papers called "malignant typhoid fever." The tribe first slaughtered dogs and burros as a sacrifice, then held a council.

In the ranchers' account, medicine men poured a boiled herb liquid down the throats of two pigeons, and when the male flew off and the female fell dying they declared that a woman of the tribe was a witch. The women were then driven in single file past the dead bird, and the first to reach for it, a daughter of a sub-chief named Creso, was seized by the medicine men. She pleaded for her life, but her own relatives helped drag her to the council place.

Semon's version mentioned no epidemic or pigeon test, saying only that the young woman had "acquired the reputation of being bewitched" and that "the head men of the band concluded to put her to death." Both versions agreed that she was stripped, tied to a stake and burned, and that she died after about two hours. In Semon's telling the Indians danced and added fuel while she screamed; the ranchers described braves dancing and medicine men muttering incantations.

The Indians told Semon that they had not burned a witch in several years, although others had been condemned and had escaped. The victim's name was not given, and no report of an arrest, an inquest or any official action appears in the coverage.

The first reports appeared on September 17, 1888, when the Sacramento Daily Record-Union printed the Semon dispatch as "INDIAN BARBARISM" and the Rock Island Daily Argus ran a short wire form, "BURNED ALIVE AS A WITCH." The pigeon-test version, datelined San Francisco, ran on September 18 in the St. Paul Daily Globe as "TORTURED BY HER TRIBE" and in the Indianapolis Journal as "AN INDIAN ATROCITY." The Washington Evening Star and the Camden Evening Telegram printed a shorter form attributed directly to the ranchers, and the Omaha Daily Bee ran Semon's account as a special telegram.

Reprints continued for weeks; the Democratic Northwest of Napoleon, Ohio, headed the story "Days of Witchcraft Revived in This Country," and the Richmond Dispatch printed the longest version on September 23. Condensed Semon paragraphs ran in Idaho and Arizona papers in October, and in mid-November the River Falls Journal of Wisconsin listed the burning among "Odd Occurrences."

The coverage called the victim a "squaw" and the tribe "redskins" and "frenzied reds." A paragraph from the New York Star, reprinted in the Pulaski Citizen of Tennessee, said the story was enough to revive the early settlers' hatred of Indians but recalled that the "same devilish cruelty" had once been practiced at Salem, Massachusetts.

The accounts differed on cause and procedure: Semon's version attributed the killing to a decision of the band's head men at Rock Springs about three weeks before September 16, while the San Francisco version tied it to an epidemic, a pigeon test and a council and gave no date. Semon was not said to have seen the burning, while the ranchers were said to have been drawn to the camp by the noise of it; the sub-chief's name was printed variously as Creso, Craso and Cresco.

reader.title: Burning of a Mojave woman accused of witchcraft (1888)
bases: Members of a Mojave band, led by its head men or medicine men, were reported to have tied a young woman accused of witchcraft to a stake and burned her to death outside any court (A1, A3).

Both accounts say a group of Mojave Indians (head men, medicine men, her relatives, dancing braves) burned the woman to death as a witch, a killing under a pretext of tradition and accusation (A1, A3); the papers describe a tribal decision and say nothing about legal authority, so illegality is not stated, and the case is an intra-tribal execution rather than a killing across racial lines.

Two separately sourced accounts, one from Frank Semon (A1) and one from unnamed ranchers (A3), agree on the core event, though both reached the press secondhand and no official confirmation appears (A1, A3).
